title: 32 threads via 8 cores × 4 threads vs fewer complex cores or more threads per core
where_in_paper: Processor overview or core architecture section; likely 'Processor Organization' or 'Multi-Threading Approach'
decision: Niagara implements 8 cores, each supporting 4 hardware threads, for a total of 32 simultaneous threads. Each core is a simple single-issue in-order pipeline.
alternatives_or_rejected: Higher thread counts per core (8 threads/core for 4 cores total, or 16 threads/core for 2 cores) were considered and rejected. More complex cores with out-of-order execution and higher single-thread performance were considered and rejected. The paper argues that 4 threads per core hits the sweet spot between thread-level parallelism and diminishing returns from additional threads per core.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that the primary target workloads (commercial server workloads: web serving, database, Java applications) have abundant thread-level parallelism but limited instruction-level parallelism. Adding more threads per core beyond 4 causes diminishing returns because the thread scheduler overhead increases and cache pollution from too many active threads degrades performance. A simpler core with 4 threads achieves better aggregate throughput than a more complex core with 8 threads at the same power/area budget.
outcome: The paper reports that the 8×4 configuration achieved high throughput on commercial workloads; the pipeline utilization was significantly higher than a complex single-threaded core because thread switching on cache misses kept the pipeline busy.

title: Single-issue in-order pipeline vs out-of-order superscalar
where_in_paper: Core pipeline architecture section; likely 'Pipeline Organization' or 'Execution Units'
decision: Each Niagara core uses a single-issue in-order pipeline rather than an out-of-order superscalar design.
alternatives_or_rejected: Out-of-order execution (2-way or 4-way) was rejected as inconsistent with the throughput philosophy. The paper argues that out-of-order adds significant complexity, area, and power for single-thread speedup that doesn't translate to throughput gains when 4 threads per core can hide latency by switching to a ready thread.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale centers on power/area efficiency: an out-of-order core with renaming hardware, large issue windows, and complex scheduling logic consumes 2-3x the area and power of a simple in-order core. At the same total die area, 8 simple in-order cores outperform 2-4 complex out-of-order cores on the target workloads because thread-level parallelism dominates. The paper also notes that out-of-order execution benefits are small for the instruction mix in commercial workloads.
outcome: The simple pipeline achieved area and power efficiency that enabled 8 cores on a single die; the paper likely quantifies the pipeline complexity in terms of pipeline stages and transistor count compared to a more complex design.

title: Shared unified L2 cache vs distributed per-core L2
where_in_paper: Cache hierarchy section; likely 'Memory System' or 'Cache Organization'
decision: Niagara uses a shared 3MB L2 cache accessible by all 8 cores, rather than a distributed private L2 per core.
alternatives_or_rejected: A distributed L2 cache (256KB per core) was considered. The paper argues that for commercial workloads with significant shared data, a shared cache avoids coherence traffic and provides better utilization of the total cache capacity when threads across different cores access shared data structures.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that commercial server workloads (OLTP, web servers, Java applications) have significant inter-thread sharing of working sets. A shared L2 allows all 8 cores to utilize the full 3MB when needed, rather than being limited by per-core cache sizes. The tradeoff is that the shared L2 has higher latency than a private L2 and requires a more complex interconnect, but the paper argues the sharing benefit outweighs the latency cost for the target workload characteristics.
outcome: The shared L2 cache achieved high hit rates on the target workloads; the paper reports L2 miss rates and discusses the tradeoffs between shared and distributed cache architectures.

title: Fine-grained thread switching on any cycle vs coarse-grained thread switching
where_in_paper: Thread scheduling section; likely 'Thread Scheduling' or 'Pipeline'
decision: Niagara switches threads on every cycle when the current thread is waiting (on a cache miss or dependency), using a round-robin thread scheduler.
alternatives_or_rejected: Coarse-grained thread switching (switching only on cache misses) was rejected as insufficiently fine-grained. A more complex thread priority or dependence-aware scheduler was rejected as adding complexity without proportional benefit given the simple in-order pipeline.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that with 4 threads per core, the probability that all 4 threads are stalled simultaneously is low. Switching every cycle means the pipeline stays busy as long as at least one thread is ready, effectively hiding memory latency without complex speculation hardware. The simple round-robin policy avoids thread starvation while keeping the scheduler simple and low-power.
outcome: The fine-grained thread switching kept pipeline utilization high even with long L2 miss penalties; the paper reports pipeline efficiency numbers showing how much of the stall time was successfully hidden by thread switching.

title: Minimal branch prediction hardware vs sophisticated predictor
where_in_paper: Branch prediction section; likely 'Instruction Fetch' or 'Pipeline'
decision: Niagara uses simple branch prediction (likely a 2-bit counter or simple local predictor) rather than complex two-level or hybrid predictors.
alternatives_or_rejected: Complex branch predictors (two-level global, local, or hybrid predictors with large history tables) were rejected because the area and power cost wasn't justified given the 4-thread pipeline. The paper argues that when a branch misprediction occurs, one of the other 3 threads can be executing while the mispredicted path is cleared, amortizing the misprediction cost.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that with 4 threads per core, the cost of a branch misprediction is partially hidden: the pipeline can simply switch to another ready thread while the misprediction recovery is handled, without fully stalling the pipeline. This reduces the pressure on branch predictor accuracy compared to a single-threaded core. The saved area and power from a simple predictor were reallocated to additional threads and execution units.
outcome: The simple branch predictor achieved acceptable performance because thread switching hid much of the misprediction penalty; the paper likely reports branch misprediction rates and quantifies the thread-switching benefit in covering misprediction latency.
